name: Kerala
summary_text: Kerala is a state within India and stands under the national transgender-rights framework, which Parliament narrowed in March 2026. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill replaced the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist; the government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking, while critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.  The national baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court of India in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have interpreted to cover gender identity: the Supreme Court has held that discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity falls within Article 15's prohibition of discrimination by sex, and the Allahabad High Court extended that in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on sexual orientation grounds. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.  Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.  Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction across the country. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been asked to take a medical exam by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.  Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans flowing from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.  Kerala's own enforcement record under the national statute is among the highest sub-national totals in India. A crime-data report of 30 January 2026 records two of the seven national Transgender Persons Act cases in 2021 as arising in Kerala, and four of the eleven in 2023, a figure joint-highest with Tamil Nadu. The report cautions that national counts are tiny because of police-registration bias, so these totals measure recorded cases rather than incidence.  Facilities and care access are set largely at state level. The Union government told Parliament in December 2021 that Kerala is among twelve states and union territories reported to have constituted Transgender Welfare Boards under Section 10(1) of the 2019 Rules. Kerala's board operates alongside those of Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra and Odisha, coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions. Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community, and in August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.  Intersex minors remain at risk. Reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.

name: Mexico
summary_text: Mexico has no national administrative procedure for legal gender recognition; the process is set state by state. As of March 2025, 22 of the 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, two more operated one in practice without legislative enactment, and six state legislatures had enacted none at all. Only seven states extend recognition to children.  In 2022 the Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states and extended the right to minors, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible procedure. Where no procedure exists, trans people are left carrying identity documents that contradict their lived gender, and that mismatch drives discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco. Recognition therefore depends on the state a person is in.  Tabasco, documented jointly by Human Rights Watch and the Community Center for Inclusion on 6 March 2024, had no legal gender-recognition procedure. There, every document request or appearance scrutiny carries risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and trans people are excluded from employment, health services, education and financial transactions.  The protective machinery is weak. More than 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022, and the Tabasco material includes the August 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gomez in Villahermosa.
